Data load and preparation before modelling

The data are the 2016 General Social Survey extract supplied in the homework template. The following preparation follows the assignment: missing values are removed before any responses are recoded.

gss16 <- read.csv("data/gss16.csv")

Cleaning and selecting columns

gss16_advfront <- gss16 %>%
  select(advfront, emailhr, educ, polviews, wrkstat) %>%
  drop_na()

Re-levelling advfront

gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    advfront = case_when(
      advfront == "Strongly agree" ~ "Agree",
      advfront == "Agree" ~ "Agree",
      TRUE ~ "Not agree"
    ),
    advfront = fct_relevel(advfront, "Not agree", "Agree")
  )

Re-levelling polviews

gss16_advfront <- gss16_advfront %>%
  mutate(
    polviews = case_when(
      str_detect(polviews, "[Cc]onservative") ~ "Conservative",
      str_detect(polviews, "[Ll]iberal") ~ "Liberal",
      TRUE ~ polviews
    ),
    polviews = fct_relevel(polviews, "Conservative", "Moderate", "Liberal")
  )

gss16_advfront %>%
  count(advfront) %>%
  mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Outcome distribution after data preparation")
Outcome distribution after data preparation
advfront n proportion
Not agree 166 0.142
Agree 1006 0.858

There are 1172 complete observations, from 2867 original rows. “Not agree” includes “Dont know” as instructed; it does not mean that every respondent in this group actively disagrees. These are observational, complete-case analyses without survey weights. Associations should not be interpreted as causal effects, and the results cannot automatically be generalised to all US adults.

Exercise 1: Create a linear regression model

Exercise 1 (a)

email_mod_1 <- lm(emailhr ~ educ, data = gss16_advfront)
email_coef_1 <- tidy(email_mod_1, conf.int = TRUE)
knitr::kable(email_coef_1, digits = 4,
             caption = "Simple linear regression coefficients")
Simple linear regression coefficients
term estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
(Intercept) -2.7573 1.6600 -1.6610 0.097 -6.0143 0.4997
educ 0.6854 0.1157 5.9238 0.000 0.4584 0.9124

The fitted line is

\[ \widehat{\text{emailhr}} = -2.757 + 0.685\,\text{educ}. \]

Each additional year of education is associated with an estimated 0.685 additional hours spent on email per week, on average. The fitted value estimates mean weekly email hours for a given education level; emailhr is the response, so there is no separate emailhr regression coefficient. The intercept is -2.757 hours at zero years of education. This negative prediction is not physically meaningful and illustrates a limitation of using a straight line for a non-negative response.

Exercise 1 (b)

email_glance_1 <- glance(email_mod_1)
# Display all columns returned by glance() in a readable vertical table.
email_glance_1 %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Statistic", values_to = "Value") %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 6, caption = "All model fit statistics from glance()")
All model fit statistics from glance()

The model has an R-squared of 0.0291, so education explains only 2.91% of the observed variation in weekly email hours. The adjusted R-squared is 0.0283. The residual standard error is 10.86 hours per week, indicating substantial unexplained variation. The overall F-test gives F(1, 1170) = 35.09 and p = 4.13e-09. Thus there is evidence of an association, but statistical significance does not imply useful predictive performance.

ggplot(gss16_advfront, aes(x = educ, y = emailhr)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, colour = "#28536B") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "#C05A32", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Years of education", y = "Email hours per week")

Weekly email hours versus years of education, with the fitted regression line. 

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 2))
plot(email_mod_1, which = c(1, 2, 3, 5))

Residual diagnostics for the simple linear regression. 

par(old_par)

The residual-versus-fitted plot shows a non-uniform vertical spread, with large positive residuals at higher fitted values. The scale-location plot also shows increasing residual spread, making constant error variance questionable. The residual smoother trends down rather than remaining horizontal around zero, which also raises doubts about the linear mean relationship. The Q-Q plot departs strongly from the reference line in the upper tail, indicating right-skewed, non-normal residuals and large outliers. The residual-versus-leverage plot helps identify observations that could influence the fitted line. The model also predicts negative hours at very low education levels.

The plots do not establish that errors are independent; this depends on the survey design, and respondents may be clustered. Overall, the low R-squared and problematic residual distribution make this model weak for individual predictions. Conventional standard errors and hypothesis tests should also be interpreted cautiously because their assumptions are questionable.
